rows: Experts may revisit earlier and later stages repeatedly rather than follow a fixed sequence.
Complexity levels remain user-selectable so learners control when additional functions appear.
Adjacent exploration occurred when the scaffold surfaced tools that were not mentioned in the tutorials.
The observed navigation pattern concerns beginners completing the two evaluated Blender task conditions while the scaffold was present.
The comparison covered one beginner-level UV-unwrapping task and one more complex walk-cycle task in Blender.
The proposed transition replaces strong scaffolding with lightweight native-interface cues as users gain skill.
Selected task-relevant tools must be organizable into meaningful workflow stages.
Structured workflow decomposition requires a task with sufficiently stable stages and can constrain divergent open-ended work.
The scaffold becomes limiting when it does not surface tools an expert expects to use.
The completion-time benefit was significant for the more demanding Task 2 but not for Task 1.
The evidence comes from 32 beginners in a fully balanced assignment with eight participants per task-interface combination.
Unified scaffolding reduces context switching while creating a risk of reduced exposure to the full application.
When a needed tool is hidden at another complexity level, familiar experts may use native shortcuts instead of advancing disclosure.
Cross-software consistency requires mappings between conceptually equivalent but operationally distinct tools that remain valid as applications evolve.
Scaffolded controls retain shortcut, menu-path, or interaction cues linking them to the native environment.
Cooperation requires meaningful learner autonomy and participation in decisions plus guidance toward positive goal interdependence.
The anticipated transfer concerns later problems sharing critical underlying features rather than merely similar surface features.
The diagnosis problem arises when tasks admit multiple equally valid solutions and routes rather than one correct step sequence.
The comparison mechanism requires reflection on a completed solution process and contrast with other problem-solving processes.
Computer-based design support may need to be combined with teacher-facilitated metacognitive and self-regulation support.
Observed computer-based implementations commonly depend on learner opt-out or predetermined removal intervals rather than continual performance diagnosis.
Students must retain choices, decision points, consequence exploration, and path selection throughout scaffold use.
For an effect of scaffolding rather than merely an effect with scaffolding, responsibility must move from the combined student–scaffold system to the student.
